_meta.title: Injection Classes
_meta.description: The everyday killers of enterprise applications: data interpreted as code or structure. Highest ROI class for a web-facing tool to master, because these vulnerabilities are everywhere and almost always reachable from HTTP.

techniques.name: SQL Injection (Union / Error Based)
techniques.summary: Craft input that terminates a string context and appends attacker SQL: union-select to exfiltrate arbitrary tables, error-based to read data through verbose database errors. Full read/write against the database backend, sometimes to RCE via sp_execute/INTO OUTFILE.

detection.description: WAF/IDS patterns for quote-terminators plus SQL keywords in parameters; anomalous 500s and database error text in responses; sudden large row-count queries from application service accounts; SELECT volume on tables the app never reads in normal flow.
mitigations: Parameterized queries / prepared statements everywhere (the actual fix)
ORM query APIs with bound parameters; never string-concatenate SQL
Least-privilege DB accounts per service; disable dangerous features (xp_cmdshell, FILE)
Generic error pages; never echo SQL error detail to clients

techniques.name: Blind SQL Injection (Boolean / Time / Out-of-Band)
techniques.summary: Extract data one bit at a time when output is not reflected: conditionals flip page content (boolean), sleep/CASE delays encode bits (time), or DNS/HTTP callbacks exfiltrate the answer (OOB). Slow, noisy in aggregate, and the most common path when error-based is suppressed.

detection.description: Request-pattern analytics: same endpoint with systematically varied parameter values, stable inter-request timing, per-character enumeration velocity; DB audit logs showing repeated information_schema queries; out-of-band DNS lookups from the DB host (the smoking gun for OOB).
mitigations: Same parameterization fix as reflected SQLi
Rate-limit and fingerprint repetitive enumeration (queries per second per session)
Egress filtering from database hosts (blocks OOB channels entirely)

techniques.name: OS Command Injection
techniques.summary: Application shells out to a system binary with user-controlled arguments; metacharacters (; | && $()) break out into arbitrary command execution under the web service account. Direct route to RCE with almost no specialized tooling required.

detection.description: Web server accounts spawning shells or binaries they never legitimately run; process ancestry violations (nginx/apache -> bash, w3wp -> cmd.exe); egress attempts immediately following parameterized requests; WAF metacharacter alerts.
mitigations: Never invoke shells from web code; use language-native libraries and strict allowlists
If unavoidable: argv-array execution, no shell, strict input allowlisting (regex ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$)
Run workers under least-privilege, no-shell-required service identities
Process-ancestry monitoring (Sysmon EID 1, Linux auditd execve) alerting on lineage breaks

techniques.name: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI)
techniques.summary: User input embedded into a template before rendering: template syntax like {{7*7}} or ${7*7} evaluates server-side, and in engines such as Jinja2/Twig/Freemarker the object graph leads to process execution (SSTI is usually RCE in an evening of work). Fingerprint the engine first, then walk its sandbox escapes.

detection.description: Responses reflecting arithmetic payloads evaluated server-side (49 instead of {{7*7}}); template engine exceptions in logs referencing user strings; process spawn under template/cache directories; poll-based WAF alerts for ${} and {{}}.
mitigations: Treat templates as code: never render user input as template source, pass it as context data
Sandboxed engines with restricted globals, deny-list of dunder/attribute chains
Alert on template-engine stack traces containing request data

techniques.name: XML External Entity Injection (XXE)
techniques.summary: If the XML parser resolves external entities, DOCTYPE definitions read local files (file://), pivot to internal services (http:// - the SSRF bridge), or exfiltrate out-of-band via parameter entities. Legacy SOAP endpoints and anything accepting XML file uploads are prime surface.

detection.description: DOCTYPE/ENTITY keywords in request bodies at WAF; local file paths appearing in application errors; XML parser library stack traces; outbound requests from the application host to internal-only addresses immediately after XML uploads.
mitigations: Disable DTDs and external entities at the parser (disallow-doctype-decl, ENTITY false) - the complete fix
Prefer JSON; where XML remains, use SAX/StAX with features locked down
Egress filtering from app tier to internal service ranges

techniques.name: Insecure Deserialization
techniques.summary: Deserializing attacker-controlled objects (Java serialized streams, .NET ViewState, PHP objects, Python pickle) instantiates gadget chains that end in code execution. ViewState without MAC validation, pre-auth Java gadget chains (Commons-Collections class), and pickle in web apps are the canonical instances.

detection.description: Serialized-object signatures in request bodies (rO0A, O:x, aca26d for .NET ViewState); ysoserial-pattern payloads at WAF; gadget-class names (InvokerTransformer, ObjectInputStream) in stack traces; heap-dump review after anomalies.
mitigations: Never deserialize untrusted data with native object formats; use JSON with strict schemas
ViewState: enforce MAC validation and latest encryption (machineKey hygiene)
Upgrade gadget-bearing libraries; monitor deserialization exceptions
RASP/runtime hooks on ObjectInputStream-style entry points for high-risk apps
